anomaly_def.Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statements or transaction boundaries are written so inefficiently that they drive the engine to process far more data or hold locks far longer than the true business requirement dictates.
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Physical table, index, or partition design does not match access patterns, forcing even well-written statements into full scans, non-covering lookups, or write-amplified index maintenance.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Allocated free space for data files, indexes, logs, or temporary areas reaches hard limits, causing allocation failures and write stalls rather than pure I/O bandwidth saturation.

Combined phenomena: When all three root causes coexist, long-running or chatty SQL generated by the application meets a schema lacking the right supporting structures, leading to massive full-table or full-index scans, spill-to-disk hash/ sort operations, and bloated intermediate results. These operations create excessive temporary segments, huge redo/transaction logs, and frequent index leaf splits, accelerating space consumption. As free space dwindles, the engine triggers emergency auto-extend, space scavenging, or outright allocation failures, which in turn prolong statement latency, trigger lock timeouts, block writers, and surface "out-of-space" errors to the application. Performance degradation and space exhaustion therefore appear together, with slow queries, intermittent write stalls, aborted DML, sudden log-archive backlog, and cascading replica lag all occurring in the same time window.

Causal chain: Inefficient workload logic inflates the volume of data read and written; the missing or ill-suited indexes magnify this volume by preventing selective access and by adding maintenance overhead on every DML. Both factors exponentially increase the size of temporary work areas, undo/redo logs, and secondary index pages. The burst of space demand rapidly consumes tablespace and log capacity, pushing the system into autogrowth events or hard space limits. Once space becomes scarce, allocation pauses and log recycling delays further slow or block the very workload that is already running long, creating a reinforcing feedback loop that degrades throughput, heightens contention, and can ultimately cause service-level outages.

entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with a general engine-level execution problem surfaced by the official error catalogue, but its precise trigger must be interpreted together with workload context and surrounding evidence.
entry.solution_guidance: Review the surrounding workload, official description, and engine state to determine whether the issue is rooted in SQL logic, resource pressure, configuration, or environmental instability.
